transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Boyd (Redwood SE), Amir Patel (Stella CTO), Lisa Gomez (ML Platform Lead), Rachel Chen (DevOps), Tom Whitaker (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, rough):
- Goal: align on POC acceptance criteria for latency/throughput SLOs, define measurement plan for TTFT vs TPOT and sampling, identify workload shape and timeline for 6-week pilot.
- Key decisions: initial SLO targets proposed by Redwood (p95 TTFT 180ms / p99 420ms for short prompts; p95 TPOT 40ms / p99 110ms), customer to validate against production histograms; pilot will test both hosted and private VPC path for comparison.
- Next steps and owners listed.

Topics (auto tags): POC scoping, TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, sampling, warm vs cold start, batching, quantization, data residency, telemetry/labels.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick off. we're here to make sure the POC has crisp acceptance criteria for latency and throughput so you can make the right go/no-go decision at the end of the pilot.
[00:12] Amir: thanks, yes, we're trying to validate that inference is cost effective at scale but also meets tight latency for our clinician UI, so star- low tail latency matters.
[00:22] Priya: quick intro from our side -- i'm priya, i'll lead the performance and measurement plan, marcus will help on the benchmark harness and infra.
[00:31] Lisa: hi all, lisa here. our key constraint is we need 99.9% of interactive sessions to feel sub-400ms for first token ideally, but there's wiggle room if cost tradeoffs are clear.
[00:45] Rachel: and we need data to stay in our VPC for PHI-sensitive flows; we'll test both hosted path and a VPC private deployment in the POC.
[00:54] Jordan: great, so for structure today, propose we: 1) agree SLOs (TTFT and TPOT percentiles), 2) define measurement methodology and sampling cadence, 3) workload sizing and test matrix (burst vs steady), and 4) timeline and handoffs.

[01:12] Tom: quick clarification - when you say TTFT you mean time to first token right? not total response time.
[01:17] Priya: right, TTFT = time from request ingress to first token emitted. TPOT stands for per-token time (we sometimes call it T P O T in notes), it's the steady-state per-token latency important for long responses.

[01:33] Amir: our typical prompts are short: median prompt length 24 tokens, median response 42 tokens, but there are spikes where clinicians request long summaries (~400 tokens).
[01:45] Jordan: that's useful. that suggests we need SLO buckets by response length: short (<64 tokens), medium (64-256), long (>256).

[02:05] Priya: propose initial SLOs (ballpark) for the pilot:
- Short responses: p95 TTFT 180ms, p99 TTFT 420ms; p95 TPOT 40ms, p99 TPOT 110ms.
- Medium: p95 TTFT 240ms, p99 700ms; p95 TPOT 45ms, p99 140ms.
- Long: p95 TTFT 400ms, p99 1.2s; p95 TPOT 55ms, p99 220ms.

[02:40] Lisa: those numbers look reasonable as a starting point. i'm worried p99s for long responses at 1.2s may still be too high for some staff, but acceptable for summaries that are async.
[02:55] Rachel: can we also capture cold-start effects? our on-call UI sometimes hits an instance after idle period.
[03:04] Marcus: yes, we'll capture warm vs cold: cold meaning fresh worker without kv cache or compiled kernels, warm meaning cached. measurement plan will include explicit cold-start test and steady-state run.

[03:20] Priya: measurement plan outline:
- Sampling: 1) offline replay of production traces for functional correctness, 2) live synthetic load to emulate traffic shapes (bursts and steady), 3) distributed client to measure client-side TTFT and server-side telemetry.
- Percentiles: we'll compute p50, p90, p95, p99 for both TTFT and TPOT, plus error rates and 95% CI over 10 runs.
- Labeling: test runs will tag by model variant, quantization (fp16/int8), batch size, route (hosted vs private), and sequence-length bucket.

[04:05] Amir: how do you handle batching? our traffic is spiky during morning rounds, so batching can help cost but might increase tail latency.
[04:14] Jordan: good point. POC will test several batching policies: none, small fixed batch (2-8), and adaptive continuous batching. we'll measure per-token cost and p95 tpots.

[04:36] Lisa: also want to see the impact of quantization on quality and latency; we care about token-level accuracy and hallucination rates.
[04:45] Priya: we'll include a quality checkpoint using a small eval set from your prompts. expect to run qualitative checks and automated divergence metrics.

[05:00] Tom: for the hosted route, are you able to show consistent pinning to model versions? we need deterministic behavior across runs.
[05:07] Jordan: yes, Redwood supports model pinning and rollout policies; for the POC we'll pin to a stable model revision for the measurement windows.

[05:20] Rachel: about telemetry and observability — what traces/labels will be available? we need token-level timestamps and request ids to join logs with our client traces.
[05:29] Marcus: we'll provide request-id propagation, per-stage timings (ingress, routing, queue, kernel exec, first token, subsequent tokens), and a cost breakdown per route. sample dashboards/Exports link will be shared.

[05:45] Amir: competitor question — we've looked at Anthropic and Vertex — why choose Redwood?
[05:52] Jordan: for this use-case Redwood emphasizes production SLO tooling: combined batching, KV cache, and routing to meet latency targets while lowering per-token cost; plus we can run private VPC for PHI.

[06:10] Lisa: timeline — what's realistic for a 6-week pilot?
[06:15] Priya: suggested timeline: week 0 onboarding and infra prep; week 1 baseline replay and short-run tests; week 2-3 stress and tunings (batching, quantization); week 4 A/B hosted vs private runs; week 5 acceptance runs and quality evals; week 6 analysis/report and go/no-go.

[06:38] Jordan: so we'll need access to your sample traffic histograms and a small sample of prompts by tomorrow ideally to build the replay.

[06:45] Amir: we can extract histograms but need to scrub PHI. we'll provide synthetic traces that mirror size and timing by 2026-11-18.

[06:55] Priya: measurement specifics — TTFT measurement: measure at the server ingress (timestamp in) to first byte emitted (first token event), but also capture client-observed first-byte to account for network. TPOT: measure average per-token interval during steady-state chunk (exclude kernel compile overhead).

[07:18] Marcus: we'll run 10 repeated steady-state runs per config to capture variance. for burst testing we'll use a poisson arrival model and a specific morning-rush shape you provide.

[07:30] Rachel: security question: for private deployment, what's the approach to KMS and audit logs? we need key control and full request audit.
[07:38] Jordan: private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and audit log streaming to your SIEM; we'll include an architecture note in the handoff.

[07:48] Lisa: can you include the SLO acceptance gating for the POC? like how many violations are allowed during acceptance run?
[07:55] Priya: propose acceptance rule: during the final acceptance window (48-hour steady-state run), each sequence-length bucket must meet p95 and p99 targets with no more than 1% of requests exceeding p99 thresholds and overall error rate <0.2%. we can make thresholds configurable.

[08:20] Tom: that seems stringent but fair. we may want a softened ramp: initial acceptance for go-to-prod vs strict for SLA contract later.

[08:33] Jordan: noted, we'll include a ramp plan in the SLO charter.

[08:40] Amir: curious about cost visualization — can the POC give projected per-1M-token cost under the tested configs?
[08:47] Marcus: yes, the benchmark harness computes per-token compute cost and we can map to your committed vs on-demand pricing assumptions; we'll include a cost-extrapolation sheet.

[09:00] Lisa: any gotchas you'd recommend we watch for?
[09:04] Priya: yes: 1) cold-start spikes if autoscaling is too slow, 2) sequence length variance causing unexpected queueing, 3) quantization regressions hurting quality — we will run quality checks alongside perf tests.

[09:22] Jordan: ok let's capture explicit deliverables. (recap) 1) Redwood provides benchmark harness + scripts; 2) Customer provides sanitized traffic histograms and sample prompt set; 3) Redwood runs hosted and private runs and shares dashboards + raw telemetry; 4) final acceptance window and report.

[09:44] Amir: agreed. i'll coordinate with lisa on the artifacts.
[09:49] Rachel: when can we meet for the SE deep dive? next week works; i'll pick two times.

[09:56] Jordan: perfect. i'll send calendar invites and upload artifacts to the shared drive.

[10:05] Priya: one small note on measurement: for p99 estimation we prefer block-bootstrapped CI over single-run p99; we'll compute confidence intervals so you can tell if differences are statistically significant.
[10:18] Lisa: appreciated. ok wrapping up—thanks everyone.

[10:26] Jordan: thanks all. action items and next steps in the meeting notes.
